note_en: Chinese verbs don't change form for the past. Instead, 了 after a verb marks a completed action: 于是他写下了几句诗 "so he wrote down a few lines of poetry." Notice that many sentences in this story have no 了 at all (他一生到处旅行 "he traveled all his life"): the past setting is already clear from context, so English past tense doesn't automatically mean Chinese 了.

sentences.en: One of them is "Viewing the Waterfall at Mount Lu": "The sun lights Incense Burner Peak, and purple mist rises; from afar I watch the waterfall hang above the stream. Its flying torrent plunges three thousand feet straight down; I wonder if the Milky Way is falling from the highest heaven." The exaggeration in the last line is so bold that it later became the classic example of hyperbole in poetry.

sentences.en: Legend has it that Li Bai, drunk in a boat, tried to embrace the moon's reflection in the water, fell in, and drowned. The story is beautiful, but it was very likely invented later; still, it captures perfectly the image later generations had of him: a poet forever faithful to the moon and to wine.

sentences.en: "Quiet Night Thoughts" isn't the only Li Bai poem Chinese children have to know by heart. Elementary school students must also memorize "Leaving Baidi City at Dawn": "At dawn I leave Baidi among the rainbow clouds; a thousand li to Jiangling, I'm back within a day. On both banks the cries of the apes never cease; my light boat has already passed ten thousand mountains."

sentences.en: Li Bai himself never compiled a definitive collection of his poems. Most of the roughly one thousand works that have come down to us survived only because people in the later Tang and Song dynasties collected and copied them out, among them his contemporary Wei Hao, who went around gathering and copying Li Bai's poems. Even so, many more works are said to have been lost forever.

sentences.en: It's a curious contradiction: a poet whose name is known all over the world, yet a huge part of whose work has vanished forever. This makes Li Bai's legacy seem both rich and incomplete: what we read is only part of the sea of poems he wrote in his day.
